idiom_name: pydantic model_dump(include=…) / Field(exclude=True); dict comprehension over dataclasses.asdict
implementation_notes: With pydantic the projection is either an argument or a field flag: model_dump(include={"id", "reference"}) and model_dump_json(exclude_none=True) select fields per call (nested selections use dictionaries, and the key '__all__' applies a rule to every collection member), while Field(exclude=True) removes a field from every serialization of that model. Without a library at all, dataclasses already provide the pieces - asdict() then a comprehension over a KEEP set, or an exclusion set - which is the entire pattern for a dict-shaped message. What replaces the classic filter object is the serializer's include/exclude contract or a one-line comprehension; a hand-written projection remains justified when the incoming message is a plain dict whose keys are only known at runtime.
code_sketch:
KEEP = {"id", "reference", "total"}

def public_view(message: dict) -> dict:            # dict-shaped payload
    return {k: message[k] for k in KEEP if k in message}

class OrderView(BaseModel):                        # or declare it on the model
    id: int
    reference: str
    internal_notes: str = Field(default="", exclude=True)

view = order.model_dump(include={"id", "reference"})
pitfalls: model_dump(include=...) filters only the serialization: the model still holds the full message in memory, and any logging, repr or error report that uses model_dump() without the argument ships the excluded fields.
A comprehension over a KEEP set silently produces a shorter message when a source key is renamed - assert the required keys (or validate with a model) so drift fails loudly.
exclude=True is not inherited by nested models that carry a field of the same name, so a field removed at the top level can reappear inside a child object.

Filtering a dict by copying top-level keys is shallow: removing a customer's email needs a nested projection, and dataclasses.asdict deep-copies the whole graph before the filter throws most of it away.
